title: Generational differences are often life-stage effects: work moves from optimism through pressure toward selective stability while housing and care reshape milestones
geography: Global; Ipsos Global Advisor survey across 30 countries and Ipsos Global Employee Experience Benchmark Database across industries, roles and regions

denominator.unit: adults under age 75 across 30 countries interviewed February 20–March 6, 2026

gen_z_home_expectation.unit: percent of Gen Z respondents saying home ownership is certain or likely during their lifetime

gen_z_marriage_expectation.value: More than one in two Gen Z respondents expect to marry

gen_z_parenthood_expectation.unit: percent of Gen Z respondents expecting to become a parent

housing_difficulty.unit: percent across 29 countries agreeing young people will struggle to get suitable housing even if they work hard and get good jobs

observations.method: Ipsos Global Advisor survey with cross-country generational comparisons; report also draws on Ipsos Housing Monitor data.
observations.uncertainty: These are expectations and attitudes, not observed homeownership, marriage or parenthood outcomes; country composition, wording and cohort definitions shape comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z, millennials, Gen X and boomers, with a specific housing comparison across age groups and 29 countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Traditional aspirations remain culturally durable even when timing and affordability are constrained; expectation should not be treated as a forecast of realized milestones.

observations.period: 2026 report; family and care across life stages

denominator.unit: countries covered by Ipsos Global Advisor comparisons; report includes qualitative and secondary demographic context

sandwiched_life_stage.value: Middle-aged adults are increasingly described as balancing care for children or adult children with care for ageing parents

elder_dependence.value: In the UK, elderly dependents are expected to outnumber child dependents
elder_dependence.unit: reported demographic projection cited by Ipsos

care_purchase_decision.value: The report notes that adult children may make purchase decisions for senior products and services

care_support_need.value: The ‘sandwiched’ group is framed as needing support that addresses time, emotional strain and eldercare navigation alongside employment

observations.method: Generational synthesis combining demographic sources, Ipsos research and market examples; the report is not a dedicated caregiver prevalence survey.
observations.uncertainty: The sandwiched-care framing identifies a life-stage mechanism but does not estimate the number of caregivers, hours of care, financial burden or causal employment effects.
observations.subgroup: Middle-aged adults caring across generations, including employees with child and elder dependents.
observations.counterinterpretation: Multigenerational care can also provide reciprocity, shared resources and meaning; burden depends on household structure, public services, income and geography.

observations.period: 2026 report; global employee experience benchmark across age bands

denominator.unit: more than 3.6 million employee-experience responses from workers aged 16 to 66+ across industries, roles and regions

lifecycle_pattern.value: Work experience is described as a recurring lifecycle: early optimism gives way to realism, pressure and eventually a more grounded, selective relationship with work

midcareer_strain.value: Ages 36–45 are characterized by high strain, workload and process barriers while job enjoyment is 77% and pride is 76%

early_career_trust.value: Ages 26–35 show a dip in positivity and trust in change as the early-career ‘honeymoon’ ends, while intent to stay rises

later_career_stability.value: Ages 46–55 show peaks in intent to stay and belonging, suggesting greater embeddedness despite continuing strain

observations.method: Analysis of Ipsos Global Employee Experience Benchmark Database, with age-band comparisons across workplace perceptions; report presents patterns as progression rather than a single generational divide.
observations.uncertainty: The database is observational and may contain differences in employer, industry, country, role and survey participation by age; age-band patterns do not identify within-person change over time.
observations.counterinterpretation: The apparent lifecycle may partly reflect cohort, occupation, selection and macroeconomic differences rather than aging itself; the report explicitly says context, culture and leadership still shape experience.

observations.period: 2026 report; work strain, respect and organizational communication

denominator.unit: more than 3.6 million employee-experience responses in the global benchmark database

squeezed_middle.value: Ages 36–45 are described as absorbing inefficiencies and process barriers rather than escalating them, with downstream effects on workplace culture

respect_perception.value: Across 30 countries, 40% of employed 16–25-year-olds often feel different age groups do not respect them, compared with 21% among 56–65-year-olds

older_communication_gap.value: Ages 56–65 lag most on timely, relevant, open and honest communication, leader response to suggestions and trust in executives

selective_engagement.value: The report describes later-career employees as more discerning and intentional, investing energy where work feels worthwhile and authentic

observations.method: Employee-experience benchmark analysis combined with a separate 30-country public perception survey of workplace age groups.
observations.uncertainty: Perceptions of respect and communication are self-reported; the report does not observe manager behavior, turnover, productivity or the organizational consequences it hypothesizes.
observations.subgroup: Employees across age bands, with emphasis on early-career, mid-career and later-career experiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age-group stereotypes may shape both expectations and responses; the same behavior can reflect role, hierarchy or tenure rather than age.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos publication context for the Generations Report 2026 and its demographic and workplace sections.
Housing Monitor context for the cross-country housing concern cited in the report.

boundary: This record adds a comparative life-stage mechanism: generational behavior should not be read only as cohort difference because care responsibilities, housing constraints, career stage, workplace friction and institutional communication evolve across the life course. The report combines a 30-country attitude survey, secondary demographic sources and a very large employee-experience benchmark; it is not a single probability sample, person-level panel, causal aging study, caregiver prevalence estimate or verified workplace outcome dataset.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official 73-page Ipsos PDF was retrieved and reviewed for Global Advisor sample scope, housing and milestone expectations, sandwich-care framing, employee-experience database size, age-band lifecycle interpretation, midcareer strain, belonging, communication and respect findings; the PDF was hashed.
